questions.prompt: What is wireless communication?
choices: Communication that can send information using radio waves
Communication that works only without the Internet
questions.explanation: Radio waves carry information without a cable between the communicating devices, so B is the example that fits. Wireless communication is not limited to satellites and does not require an Internet connection; other wireless media also exist.

evidence.title: IEEE 802.11: wireless LAN standards

questions.prompt: How many bits are in 1 Byte?
questions.explanation: One byte contains eight bits. A bit is a single binary digit; a byte groups eight of them. Keep the capital B in MB separate from the lowercase b in Mb when converting file sizes and transmission rates.

evidence.title: NIST: bytes and decimal/binary prefixes

questions.prompt: How many layers are in the OSI model?
questions.explanation: The OSI reference model has seven layers, from Physical to Application. Do not confuse this conceptual model with common four- or five-layer presentations of the Internet protocol stack.

evidence.title: ITU-T X.200: OSI basic reference model, clause 7

questions.prompt: Which OSI layer sends bits through radio waves, cables, or other physical media?
questions.explanation: The Physical layer represents bits as signals on a medium, such as radio, copper or fibre. The Network layer handles routing; it does not define the physical signal that crosses the link.

evidence.title: ITU-T X.200: OSI basic reference model, clause 7

questions.prompt: Which OSI layer works with IP addresses and routing?
questions.explanation: The Network layer handles logical addressing and routing between networks, which is where IP fits. The Data Link layer handles frames on a link; the Transport layer handles communication between endpoints above IP.

evidence.title: ITU-T X.200: OSI basic reference model, clause 7

questions.prompt: Who standardizes Wi-Fi technology?
questions.explanation: IEEE develops the 802.11 wireless LAN standards underlying Wi-Fi. Standard development is distinct from Wi-Fi Alliance interoperability certification. The other organizations listed do not develop the 802.11 standards.

evidence.title: IEEE 802.11: wireless LAN standards

questions.prompt: What was the main service provided by 1G mobile networks?
questions.explanation: First-generation cellular systems primarily carried analog voice calls. Digital mobile communication came with 2G; high-rate Internet access and streaming belong to later developments, not the main 1G service.

evidence.title: Ericsson: history of mobile Internet

questions.prompt: What is the name of the base station in a 3G UMTS network?
questions.explanation: In UMTS, the radio base station is called Node B. An RNC controls radio resources and Node Bs; BSC is the controller name used in GSM, not the UMTS base-station name.

evidence.title: 3GPP TS 25.401: UTRAN architecture, definitions and clause 6
ETSI TR 100 053: GSM architecture, section 5.3.3

questions.prompt: In a mobile network, frequency mainly tells us:
choices: Where the signal is located in the radio spectrum
questions.explanation: Frequency measures cycles per second and identifies a signal’s place in the radio spectrum. It is different from a transmission’s time slot, the number of subscribers, or a phone’s battery level.

evidence.title: 3GPP TS 45.002: radio channels and TDMA, clauses 4.2–4.3

questions.prompt: What is fading?
choices: A change in signal strength caused by distance or obstacles
questions.reviewNote: Prepared key retained as the closest available choice(s). The original wording is broader than the technical distinction; instructor intent and the original photo remain unverified. See the explanation and primary evidence.
questions.explanation: A is the closest choice. Distance mainly changes mean path loss; obstacles cause shadowing, also called shadow fading. Multipath creates further signal variations. The option groups several propagation mechanisms under a broad use of fading; the other options are unrelated.

evidence.title: 3GPP TR 38.901: path loss, shadow fading and fast fading, clauses 7.4–7.5

questions.prompt: What is interference?
choices: Signals affecting each other when they share the wireless medium
Connecting a phone using a USB cable
questions.explanation: Unwanted radio signals can disrupt reception of a desired signal, so B fits. Sharing a medium does not always corrupt transmissions: stations may coordinate or wait for airtime. Interference concerns reception, not battery capacity or byte conversion.

evidence.title: Cisco mesh guide: co-channel interference and CSMA deferral

questions.prompt: What is one main function of a BSC in a 2G network?
questions.explanation: The GSM Base Station Controller manages base stations and radio resources within the base-station subsystem. A BSC is a network control element; it does not replace the mobile handset or perform its storage functions.

evidence.title: ETSI TR 100 053: GSM architecture, section 5.3.3

questions.prompt: Which two elements mainly form UTRAN in a 3G UMTS network?
questions.explanation: Choose A once: that option already contains both required elements, Node B and RNC. Node B provides the radio link and the RNC controls radio resources. BTS and BSC are the corresponding GSM terms, not the UMTS pair.

evidence.title: 3GPP TS 25.401: UTRAN architecture, definitions and clause 6
ETSI TR 100 053: GSM architecture, section 5.3.3

questions.prompt: Which statements correctly compare 2G and 4G?
choices: 2G commonly uses circuit switching for voice
2G was designed mainly for high-speed video streaming
questions.explanation: Choose A and C. GSM-era 2G commonly uses circuit-switched voice; LTE/EPS uses a packet-based architecture. Both are digital generations. GPRS also added packet data to 2G, so the contrast does not mean 2G can never carry packets.

evidence.title: IETF RFC 6459: GPRS and Evolved Packet System, sections 3.1 and 4.1
Ericsson: history of mobile Internet

questions.prompt: A 24 MB photo is sent in 3 seconds. What is the transmission speed?
questions.explanation: Rate = size ÷ time = 24 MB ÷ 3 s = 8 MB/s, so choose C. The question asks for bytes per second. Multiplying by eight gives 64 Mbps; mixing MB/s with Mbps is the main trap.

evidence.title: NIST: bytes and decimal/binary prefixes

questions.prompt: A file is 100 MB and the download speed is 20 MB/s. How long will the download take?
questions.explanation: Time = size ÷ rate = 100 MB ÷ 20 MB/s = 5 s, so choose B. The MB units cancel. No bits-to-bytes conversion is needed because both supplied quantities already use bytes.

evidence.title: NIST: bytes and decimal/binary prefixes

questions.prompt: A 1 GB file is downloaded using a 100 Mbps connection. Assume 1 GB = 1000 MB. What is the theoretical download time?
questions.explanation: Using the stated decimal convention, 1 GB = 1000 MB = 8000 Mb. Time = 8000 Mb ÷ 100 Mb/s = 80 s, so choose C. Ten seconds would incorrectly treat bytes as bits. This ideal estimate ignores protocol overhead.

evidence.title: NIST: bytes and decimal/binary prefixes

questions.prompt: One old cell has a radius of 50 km. New cells have a radius of 5 km. Approximately how many smaller cells are needed to cover the same area?
questions.explanation: For the same cell shape, area is proportional to radius squared. The ideal count is (50/5)² = 100, so choose D. Ten is only the radius ratio. Real coverage needs planning for overlap, terrain and interference.

evidence.title: Recorded past-paper prompt: supplied values and assumptions

questions.prompt: A 1G phone uses 18 W during a call, while a 2G phone uses 6 W. A person talks for 1.5 hours every day. How much energy is saved in one week by using the 2G phone?
questions.explanation: Saved power is 18 − 6 = 12 W. Weekly call time is 1.5 × 7 = 10.5 h. Saved energy = 12 × 10.5 = 126 Wh, so choose C. Watts measure power; watt-hours measure energy.

evidence.title: NIST: watt is a joule per second

questions.prompt: A 1G system costs $60,000 per year and serves 30 users. A 2G system costs $120,000 and serves 150 users. Which system has the lower annual cost per user?
questions.reviewNote: The calculation assumes the second stated cost is annual, as implied by the question. Original wording is preserved.
questions.explanation: Treating both supplied costs as annual costs, 1G costs $60,000/30 = $2,000 per user per year; 2G costs $120,000/150 = $800. Choose B. Compare cost per user, not just the total bill. The second cost’s annual basis is implicit in the prompt.

evidence.title: Recorded past-paper prompt: supplied values and assumptions

questions.prompt: What is the correct encapsulation order when data is sent through the network?
questions.explanation: For the usual TCP example, application data becomes a transport segment, an IP packet, a link frame, then transmitted bits. Choose C. The reverse sequence describes reception; UDP uses the term datagram rather than TCP segment.

evidence.title: ITU-T X.200: OSI basic reference model, clause 7
IETF RFC 9293: TCP transport and segments, sections 2.2 and 3.1

questions.prompt: Which situations can make a wireless connection worse?
choices: A large obstacle between the phone and base station
Adding more RAM to the phone
Many wireless users using the same radio resources
questions.explanation: Choose B and D. An obstacle can attenuate the radio path; active users share finite radio resources. Heavy load can cause airtime contention, with interference also possible. Extra storage or RAM does not by itself remove these radio limitations.

evidence.title: 3GPP TR 38.901: path loss, shadow fading and fast fading, clauses 7.4–7.5
Cisco mesh guide: co-channel interference and CSMA deferral

questions.prompt: Which sequence best describes a device connecting to Wi-Fi?
questions.explanation: B gives the simplified initial sequence: discover an access point, perform 802.11 authentication, associate, then transfer data. A protected WLAN also needs its security exchanges before protected traffic. Initial 802.11 authentication is not the same as later enterprise EAP authentication.

evidence.title: Cisco: 802.11 association and WPA/WPA2 security exchanges

questions.prompt: What happens during a Wi-Fi security handshake such as the WPA2 4-Way Handshake?
choices: Security keys are established for protected communication
The Wi-Fi password is sent openly to everyone
The client and access point confirm information needed for secure communication
The router changes its SSID automatically
questions.explanation: Choose A and C. The WPA2 four-way handshake derives and confirms transient key material and prepares protected communication. It does not broadcast the Wi-Fi passphrase or change the SSID. Authentication and key establishment should not be confused with sending a password in the clear.

evidence.title: Cisco: 802.11 association and WPA/WPA2 security exchanges

questions.prompt: A student is far from a base station, there is a large building between them, and many users are using the same wireless resources. Which two problems are most likely?
questions.reviewNote: Prepared key retained as the closest available choice(s). The original wording is broader than the technical distinction; instructor intent and the original photo remain unverified. See the explanation and primary evidence.
questions.explanation: B and C are the expected choices from this list. Distance and a building suggest path loss and shadowing; active users compete for radio resources. These clues alone do not establish fast fading or harmful interference. Compression and encapsulation are data-handling operations, not these radio effects.

evidence.title: 3GPP TR 38.901: path loss, shadow fading and fast fading, clauses 7.4–7.5
Cisco mesh guide: co-channel interference and CSMA deferral

questions.prompt: Which is an example of mobile communication?
choices: Making a call using a mobile phone
Connecting two computers only with a USB cable
questions.explanation: A mobile-phone call uses a radio link between a mobile device and the cellular network, so A fits. Reading or writing on paper does not exchange information over that link; a USB-only connection is wired.

evidence.title: 3GPP TS 25.401: UTRAN architecture, definitions and clause 6

questions.prompt: 1 millisecond is equal to:
questions.explanation: Milli means 10⁻³ and micro means 10⁻⁶. Therefore 1 ms = 10³ µs = 1000 µs, so choose C. A microsecond is the smaller unit, so a millisecond contains many of them.

evidence.title: NIST: SI prefixes, section 4.3

questions.prompt: Which OSI layer commonly uses TCP and UDP?
questions.explanation: TCP and UDP provide transport services above IP, so choose the Transport layer. TCP provides a reliable byte stream; UDP does not provide TCP’s delivery guarantees. IP addressing and routing belong to the Network layer.

evidence.title: ITU-T X.200: OSI basic reference model, clause 7
IETF RFC 9293: TCP transport and segments, sections 2.2 and 3.1

questions.prompt: Which OSI layer can be responsible for formatting, compression, and encryption?
questions.explanation: The Presentation layer describes representation and transformation of data, including formatting, compression and encryption, so A fits the OSI model. In real systems, encryption can also be implemented at other layers; the answer is a conceptual classification, not an exclusive rule.

evidence.title: ITU-T X.200: OSI basic reference model, clause 7
ITU-T X.800: Presentation layer security, clauses 7.6.1–7.6.2

questions.prompt: Wi-Fi is:
questions.explanation: Wi-Fi is a wireless local-area networking technology based on IEEE 802.11. It is a way to connect devices over a wireless link, not a battery or operating system. A Wi-Fi link can exist even without Internet access.

evidence.title: IEEE 802.11: wireless LAN standards

questions.prompt: Which technology came before 1G cellular networks?
questions.explanation: Pre-cellular mobile radio systems came before cellular generations, so choose C. Early mobile telephone services existed before 1G cellular networks. LTE, 4G and 5G are later developments, not predecessors of 1G.

evidence.title: Ericsson: first mobile telephone networks

questions.prompt: What was an important improvement of 2G compared with 1G?
questions.explanation: 2G introduced digital cellular communication in place of the analog radio voice systems associated with 1G. Voice remained supported, and messaging became an important service. Digital does not mean that mobile calls or messaging were removed.

evidence.title: Ericsson: history of mobile Internet

questions.prompt: What does UMTS stand for?
questions.explanation: UMTS expands to Universal Mobile Telecommunications System. It names the 3G system whose UTRAN uses Node B and RNC elements. The other choices resemble the acronym but are not its standardized expansion.

evidence.title: 3GPP TS 25.401: UTRAN architecture, definitions and clause 6

questions.prompt: How does TDMA separate different users?
choices: By giving users different time slots
By giving every user a different battery
By changing the phone screen size
questions.explanation: Time Division Multiple Access separates transmissions into time slots. Users can share a carrier by transmitting at different times. Do not confuse this with FDMA, which separates users by frequency channels.

evidence.title: 3GPP TS 45.002: radio channels and TDMA, clauses 4.2–4.3

questions.prompt: How does FDMA separate different users?
questions.explanation: Frequency Division Multiple Access separates users by assigning different frequency channels. TDMA instead separates transmissions in time. Phone brand, password and screen size are not radio multiple-access resources.

evidence.title: 3GPP TS 45.002: radio channels and TDMA, clauses 4.2–4.3

questions.prompt: What is one important function of the RNC in a 3G network?
choices: It controls Node B base stations and radio resources
It displays videos on the phone
questions.explanation: The Radio Network Controller manages Node Bs and radio resources in UTRAN, so choose A. Node B supplies the radio-facing base-station functions. The RNC is network infrastructure, not a handset display, photo store or SIM replacement.

evidence.title: 3GPP TS 25.401: UTRAN architecture, definitions and clause 6

questions.prompt: What does a base station mainly do?
choices: Provides a radio connection between mobile devices and the network
questions.explanation: A base station provides the radio-side connection between mobile devices and the wider network. That communication role is different from charging a handset or managing the user’s applications and accounts.

evidence.title: 3GPP TS 25.401: UTRAN architecture, definitions and clause 6

questions.prompt: A 50 MB file is transferred in 5 seconds. What is the speed?
questions.explanation: Rate = size ÷ time = 50 MB ÷ 5 s = 10 MB/s, so choose B. This is a byte rate. If requested in megabits per second it would be 80 Mbps; do not change units without the factor of eight.

evidence.title: NIST: bytes and decimal/binary prefixes

questions.prompt: A connection works at 80 Mbps. Approximately how many MB/s is this?
questions.explanation: There are eight bits per byte. Convert 80 Mbps to a byte rate by dividing by eight: 80/8 = 10 MB/s, so choose C. Keeping the number 80 while changing b to B would make the rate eight times too large.

evidence.title: NIST: bytes and decimal/binary prefixes

questions.prompt: A 400 MB video is downloaded at 80 Mbps. How long will it theoretically take?
questions.explanation: First put size and rate in the same units: 400 MB × 8 = 3200 Mb. Time = 3200 Mb ÷ 80 Mb/s = 40 s, so choose C. Five seconds misses the byte-to-bit conversion. Theoretical time excludes overhead.

evidence.title: NIST: bytes and decimal/binary prefixes

questions.prompt: A network originally uses cells with a radius of 20 km. The new system uses cells with a radius of 5 km. Approximately how many new cells are needed to cover the area of one old cell?
questions.explanation: Comparable cell areas scale with radius squared. The count is (20/5)² = 16, so choose C. Four is the radius ratio, not the area ratio. This is an ideal area estimate rather than a complete radio coverage design.

evidence.title: Recorded past-paper prompt: supplied values and assumptions

questions.prompt: Phone A uses 12 W during a call. Phone B uses 4 W. A user talks for 2 hours. How much less energy does Phone B use during that time?
questions.explanation: The power difference is 12 − 4 = 8 W. Over 2 h, the energy saving is 8 × 2 = 16 Wh, so choose C. Eight watts is a power difference; the question asks for energy over the stated duration.

evidence.title: NIST: watt is a joule per second

questions.explanation: Choose A and B: GSM is associated with 2G and LTE with the 4G era. Both use digital communication. 2G began with voice-focused services and was not designed primarily for high-definition video streaming.

evidence.title: IETF RFC 6459: GPRS and Evolved Packet System, sections 3.1 and 4.1
Ericsson: history of mobile Internet

questions.prompt: Which is the correct order of data units at the sender?
questions.explanation: At the sender in the conventional TCP example, data is wrapped into a segment, then an IP packet, then a link frame, and finally represented as bits. Choose A. Reception reverses the process; UDP’s transport unit is called a datagram.

evidence.title: ITU-T X.200: OSI basic reference model, clause 7

questions.prompt: A student walks behind a thick concrete building and the mobile signal suddenly becomes weaker. What is the best explanation?

questions.prompt: Twenty Wi-Fi devices are using the same wireless channel in a small room. Network performance becomes worse. What is the most likely problem?
questions.reviewNote: Prepared key retained as the closest available choice(s). The original wording is broader than the technical distinction; instructor intent and the original photo remain unverified. See the explanation and primary evidence.
questions.explanation: A is the expected label among these choices. questions.prompt: Which statements describe packet switching?

It can only be used for analog voice
questions.explanation: Choose A and C. Packet switching carries data in packets while multiple flows share network resources. It does not require a dedicated physical circuit for each flow. Packets carry digital information; the method is not restricted to analog voice.

choices: C ≈ 17.30 Mbps; capacity decreases at 5 dB
C = 50 Mbps; capacity increases at 5 dB

questions.explanation: 10 dB corresponds to SNRlinear = 10. C = 5 × 10⁶ log₂(11) ≈ 17.297 Mbps. Reducing SNR reduces log₂(1 + SNR), so capacity decreases.

choices: Link B, because lower SNR means less noise

questions.prompt: A transmitter radiates 100 mW at 2.4 GHz over a 20 m free-space link. Assume Gₜ = Gᵣ = 1 (linear). Compute wavelength λ, free-space path loss (dB), and received power in dBm.
questions.originalPrompt: A transmitter radiates 100 mW at 2.4 GHz over a 20 m free-space link. Assume Gₜ = Gᵣ = 1 (linear). Compute wavelength λ, free-space path loss (dB), and received power in dBm.
choices: λ ≈ 1.25 m; FSPL ≈ 6.61 dB; Pᵣ ≈ 13.39 dBm
questions.explanation: Using c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s: λ = c/f = 0.125 m. FSPL = 20 log₁₀(4πd/λ) ≈ 66.07 dB. 100 mW = 20 dBm; unity antenna gains = 0 dBi, so Pᵣ = 20 − 66.07 = −46.07 dBm.

Power becomes one quarter; loss of about 6.02 dB
Power is unchanged; loss of 0 dB
questions.explanation: Friis gives Pᵣ ∝ 1/d². Doubling distance gives (20/40)² = 1/4 of the received power. Loss = 10 log₁₀(4) ≈ 6.02 dB.
